rounds.proof_sketch: block_size = 256 (hardcoded), so threadIdx.x ∈ [0, 255]. All shared_mem accesses use indices tid or tid+stride where max(tid+stride) = 127+128 = 255. Index 256 in mutated array is never touched.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes shared memory allocation from 256 to 257 floats, but this extra element at index 256 is never accessed. The kernel uses block_size=256 (hardcoded in host code), meaning threadIdx.x ranges from 0-255. All shared memory accesses are via shared_mem[tid] (indices 0-255) or shared_mem[tid+stride] during reduction. The maximum index accessed is tid+stride when tid=127 and stride=128, giving index 255. The extra shared memory element is allocated but completely unused, making the mutation semantically equivalent regardless of input values.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable under fixed-shape contract. The mutation only adds unused shared memory allocation - no input value pattern can cause different behavior since index 256 is never read or written. Would require changing block_size to >256 threads to potentially access the difference.
rounds.recommendations: Mutation testing for array size changes should distinguish between allocation size changes that affect accessible indices vs those that only add unreachable capacity. This mutant survives because the shared memory array size exceeds the block size, but the kernel logic never accesses beyond the number of threads per block.
